rows: 25 places · the signature of Potong Pasir & MacPherson

rows.w: Young hawkerpreneur Douglas Ng rebuilt his grandmother's recipe into a hawker-fame story — soft, bouncy fishballs made from pure yellowtail with no added flour that won a Michelin Bib Gourmand in 2016; after stints at Golden Mile and Timbre+, the stall settled at Blk 77 Circuit Road in MacPherson.

Opened by former local actor Huang Yiliang, this humble evening-only stall cooks each bowl of crab bee hoon to order, drawing out a deeply sweet seafood broth — with a steamed fish and homemade omelette that regulars rate just as highly. A cult name of the renovated Circuit Road hawker centre.

A Potong Pasir prawn-noodle institution first established in 1971 and now second-generation, named for the ancestral province of founder Png Kim Soon. The broth is built from fried prawn shells and pork ribs simmered eight hours, served across a sprawling 20-dish menu of prawn, pork rib, intestine, baby abalone and clam combinations.

An old-school Hokkien mee (from S$4) simmered and fried in prawn-head and pork stock with egg, prawn, pork and yellow noodles, then left to stew so the strands soak up the umami — a repeatedly-listed Circuit Road favourite the food blogs queue for.

Victor's vegetarian satay — grilled mock-meat skewers at around S$1 a stick — draws long lines from residents and non-vegetarians alike, alongside otah and a spread of meat-free hawker classics that regularly headline Circuit Road stall guides.

The uncle who dances to instrumental music as he fries — his char kway teow is cooked with less oil than most and can be topped with a soft-boiled egg or omelette (about S$5), a Circuit Road performance-and-plate that the SPH food titles keep naming.

An ex-Hyatt manager's stall cooking authentic Seremban, Malaysia dishes — springy cuttlefish bee hoon (lai fen) with sweet sauce and a rich pork curry. After its beloved hole-in-the-wall Potong Pasir Ave 3 coffeeshop closed in March 2024, it reopened bigger and air-conditioned at The Commerze @ Irving in Sept 2024, on the MacPherson/Tai Seng edge.

An outlet of the famed fried-chicken-wing name some rate the best in Singapore — light, crackly skin over juicy meat — one of the established brands that anchored the new Woodleigh Village Hawker Centre when it opened in Sept 2024.

One of the last hawker stalls in Singapore still selling noodles from S$2.50 — old-school bak chor mee and fishball noodles tossed in chilli-and-mushroom sauce with handmade wontons. The senior couple, at Circuit Road since 2006 (the name comes from stall no.10 at NUS Engineering's canteen), keep the price down for the neighbourhood's elderly; Mothership profiled their refusal to raise it.

Opened by an apprentice of a famous bak chor mee master, this Tai Thong Crescent coffeeshop stall turns out an old-school minced-pork noodle — vinegary, lard-slicked, with fresh pork liver — that veteran hawker bloggers rank among the area's best.

A rare Henghua (Putian)-style white lor mee — a velvety, savoury (not dark) broth loaded with seafood, pork and vegetables — one of the standout regional-Chinese stalls the food guides pick out at Woodleigh Village.

A single-dish lor mee stall that has sustained itself since the 1970s on one bowl done well — a strong, savoury, gently vinegary gravy with crispy fried yam and plain hard-boiled egg, the thick starchy sauce slurpable to the last. From S$3, with a bigger S$5 portion; the boss is famously courteous.

rows: 7 places · the top tier, graded within each area

rows.w: Young hawkerpreneur Douglas Ng rebuilt his grandmother's recipe into a hawker-fame story — soft, bouncy fishballs made from pure yellowtail with no added flour that won a Michelin Bib Gourmand in 2016; after stints at Golden Mile and Timbre+, the stall settled at Blk 77 Circuit Road in MacPherson.

ITE culinary grads Darryl and Shi Long bring affordable European dining to a hawker stall — their best-selling duck confit (S$12) is a fork-tender leg on fluffy mash in a moat of rich house sauce, plus truffle pasta — a headline act of the new Woodleigh Village Hawker Centre.

Completed 1984, these steep red-pitched roofs are Singapore's most visually distinctive HDB silhouette — a mid-1980s experiment in postmodern public housing that borrowed the Malay kampong-house form to break from the usual slab blocks. Top-floor units get soaring 5-5.5 m ceilings, and Block 142's 'welcome' sign has become the emblem of the whole estate.

A 13-hectare urban park opened 3 September 2024 on the former Bidadari burial grounds, centred on Alkaff Lake — a stormwater-retention pond inspired by the colonial-era Alkaff Lake Gardens — with a 700 m Heritage Walk. Developed jointly by HDB, NParks, PUB and the National Heritage Board as the green heart of the new Bidadari estate.

Built in 1932 by Syed Abdul Rahman Alkaff of the prominent Hadhrami-Arab merchant family, this small mosque on the Potong Pasir/Bidadari edge is distinguished by a pencil-thin Ottoman-style minaret unlike any other in Singapore. Restored in 2014 and gazetted the same year as Singapore's 68th National Monument.

A value-for-money zi char stall in a MacPherson Lane coffeeshop that went viral for restaurant-grade shellfish at hawker prices — crab claws at S$5 each (four kam-heong claws for S$20), salted-egg crab around S$30 — and, unexpectedly, one of the better Penang-style char kway teow around, which is what drew ieatishootipost.

rows.n: Yi Jia South Village Seafood Restaurant
rows.w: A zi char that grew from a Toa Payoh coffeeshop into a full seafood restaurant on MacPherson Road, famed for its signature honeydew prawns — wild-caught ang kah prawns in a secret honeydew-melon sauce, served inside the melon itself — plus salted-egg crab and curry fish head. A long-running favourite of the veteran hawker bloggers.

The civic heart of the new Bidadari estate: a three-storey mall opened May 2023 (officially November 2023) integrated with the Bidadari Community Club, a neighbourhood police centre, the Woodleigh Village Hawker Centre and Woodleigh MRT — nature-inspired gathering spaces knit into the adjacent Bidadari Park and Alkaff Lake.

Young hawkerpreneur Xiao Xuan and her mother's donburi stall (started 2022 at Bukit Canberra) brings Japanese rice bowls under S$10 to Woodleigh Village — a Caramelised Char Siew Don (S$7) of smoky-sweet pork belly with a sous-vide egg, plus mentaiko chicken katsu and Angus sukiyaki dons.

Young hawker Nam's halal-certified fried-rice specialist at Woodleigh Village, plating several styles — Egg Fried Rice (S$3.20), sambal, curry and hae bee hiam — from a stall HungryGoWhere featured in its 'Hawker Hustlers' series. One of the young-entrepreneur stalls that defined the new centre.

A claypot specialist whose range runs from smoked-duck rice and barbecue-pork rice to pig trotters and bak kut teh, with a classic claypot chicken rice around S$7 — a hearty Circuit Road standby featured across the SPH stall round-ups.

A third-generation hawker cooking fried oyster, orh luak (oyster omelette) and fried carrot cake from a family recipe handed down by his grandfather — an old-school Circuit Road wok stall the SPH lifestyle titles both flag.

The hawker centre's sole vegetarian stall, run by Darryl Tong, plating a menu that reads nothing like a typical meat-free spread — 'char siew' kolo mee, fried fish bee hoon and kway chap done entirely vegan.

A Mexican stall bringing hearty rice bowls and tacos to hawker prices — part of the wave of young, cross-cuisine entrepreneurs that made Woodleigh Village one of Singapore's most internationally varied hawker centres.
